The United States debt agreement disappointed the markets and the subsequent loss of confidence helped to boost gold to new highs; a correction is likely before further strength towards year-end** Gold, the Swiss franc and the yen gathered increasing traction as safe haven assets during July and in early August as the European authorities grappled with persistent debt contagion and bail-out considerations, while the friction in the United States over the domestic debt ceiling became seen as increasingly political rather than economic. In the event the eleventh-hour deal in the United States was widely seen as unsatisfactory and gold soared to new all-time highs in the majority of currencies, posting a gain of $53 (2.7%) over 24 hours to register a fix of $1,669.25 on the morning of 3rd August. This represented a gain of 12% since the start of July and a year-on-year increase of 40%. Prices then moved higher later in the first week of August as the European Central Bank not only announced that its accommodative monetary stance would be maintained, but that more liquidity would be supplied into the market, with execution in the second week of August via a fixedrate tender (six-month maturity) with full allotment. This, combined with a poor weekly unemployment number from the United States drove gold towards $1,680. The subsequent slump in equities amid a crisis of confidence then propelled gold through $1,750 in heavy trading volume. ##### **The major underlying factors that sent gold to its highs** This short term early-August move was driven not only by the views held in some quarters that the United States debt deal was a disappointment, but also that it raised renewed questions over the possibility of a third round of quantitative easing. Significantly, although ratings agencies Moody’s and Fitch affirmed the United States credit rating at AAA following the agreement to raise the debt ceiling (but Moody’s placed the country on a negative outlook) Standard & Poor’s reduced the rating to AA+ on 5th August; equities weakened further in response and gold pierced $1,750. On the other side of the Atlantic, Moody’s had also put Spain‘s credit rating on review at the end of July, in response to concerns over Spain’s “subdued” economic growth and expanding balance sheet. In addition the nervo

usness over European sovereign debt has been reflected in local bond markets, with yields on Spanish and Italian bonds exceeding 6% in early August, the highest level for the latter country since it joined the European System of Central Banks. German bunds, by contrast, have been in demand and the spread for Italian and Spanish bond yields over those in Germany has been causing concern. In early August the spread was approaching 400 basis points and there were fears that if this persisted for an extended period of time then Spain might need to request a rescue package. The subsequent ECB intervention in the bond markets has reduced Spanish and Italian yields, and may alleviate some of this risk.
